Because they penetrate the visible surface of a painting, ultraviolet and other nonvisible spectra of
light enable the detection of otherwise imperceptible features of the work. Beneath the surface of
Claude Monet’s Wisteria $(1917-20)$, art historians found that Monet had initially included water
lilies but ultimately painted over them. Furthermore, nonvisible spectra can be used for chemical
analysis to identify specific pigments and thus, in some cases, reveal forgeries: if, for example,
titanium oxide—which wasn’t developed until the 20th century—is evident throughout the layers
of a painting attributed to an 18th-century artist, that work can only be a forgery.
